summary: Lists the design principles, scope and requirements for what became the XML Digital Signature specification. It covers requirements for the signature syntax, data model, format, cryptographic processing, and coordination with outside efforts. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a house you write down what it must have. This is the must-have list for a way to sign XML files digitally.

questions: what must xml digital signatures support
how should xml signatures handle multiple algorithms
what must xml signatures apply to
subtitle: Requirements for digitally signing and authenticating XML content

tldr.problem: As XML became a standard way to represent data, there was no standard way to digitally sign XML documents or verify the authenticity of XML content.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists the design principles and requirements that a XML digital signature specification must meet, covering the signature syntax, data model, cryptographic algorithms, and format standards.
tldr.outcome: These requirements became the foundation for the XML Digital Signature specification, which allows content creators to sign XML documents and proves the content has not been altered.

today: RFC 2807 is informational and has not been obsoleted. The XML Digital Signature specification it describes was published in 2002 as RFC 3075 and later updated; the requirements it lists remain foundational to XML security work.

sections.title: What XML Signatures Need to Do
sections.content:
XML is a standard way to store and exchange data on the internet. The mission described in this RFC is to develop a way to sign XML documents so that people can prove three things: the content has not been changed (integrity), who created it (authentication), and that the creator cannot deny sending it (non-repudiation). This RFC lists all the requirements such a system must meet without specifying how to build it.

The requirements cover the overall scope of the work, what the signature syntax must support, what the data model must handle, what cryptographic algorithms to use, and how different standards need to coordinate with each other.
sections.plainLanguage: Before building something, you write down what it must do. This RFC says a digital signature system for XML must prove content is real and unchanged, and it must work with all kinds of data.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
The requirements start with eight fundamental design principles. First, the system must work for signing digital content, especially XML. Second, XML signatures are generated from a hash over the canonical (standard) form of what is being signed. Third, the meaning is straightforward: the signature ties the content of resources to a key through a strong one-way mathematical transformation.

The system must be extensible to support different trust models and applications. The specification should not define trust semantics but rather the syntax and rules for communicating that a signature is valid. The specification should define at least one method for canonicalizing and hashing signatures, and applications must conform to XML standards like XML namespaces, XLink, and XPointer when they use them in signature syntax.

Finally, XML Signatures should be built on the broader Web design philosophy of decentralization, URIs, and modularity, taking advantage of existing cryptographic standards.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature system must be simple and fair: it proves content is real without claiming to understand trust. It should use the same rules as the rest of XML and reuse math that already works.

sections.title: What a Signature Must Support
sections.content:
The RFC requires that XML signature data structures be based on the RDF data model, though they do not need to use RDF's serialization syntax. Signatures must apply to any content addressable by a locator, including non-XML content. They must work on a part or all of an XML document.

Multiple signatures must be able to exist over the same content using different keys and algorithms. XML Signatures are first-class objects, meaning they can themselves be referenced and signed. The system must support varied digital signature and message authentication codes, including symmetric and asymmetric schemes, and resources and algorithms must be addressable by URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature system must sign any content, sign just parts of documents, allow multiple signatures, and let signatures sign other signatures.

sections.title: Format and Cryptographic Requirements
sections.content:
An XML Signature must be an XML element, preserving the document structure when signatures are added. The system must support composite documents (built by adding or deleting signed components) while maintaining integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation. Signatures can be detached (outside the document), embedded within the document, or encapsulating content.

Cryptographically, the system must permit arbitrary signature and message authentication algorithms, and must specify at least one mandatory-to-implement algorithm for signature canonicalization, content canonicalization, hashing, and signing. The design must prevent weak implementations susceptible to downgrade or algorithm substitution attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature must be part of XML, not break the document, and must pick at least one strong math method that works for everyone.

sections.title: Working with Other Standards
sections.content:
The RFC requires that XML Signature specifications meet the requirements of real-world applications including Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP), Financial Services Markup Language, and at least one forms application. To ensure requirements are met, designated reviewers from related communities must examine the specification, including the XML Syntax Working Group for canonicalization, the XML Linking Working Group for signature referents, and the XML Schema Working Group for signature schema design.

Additional review is needed from the Metadata Coordination Group, W3C Internationalization Interest Group, XML Package Working Group, and XML Fragment Working Group. This ensures the signature specification works well with other XML technologies and can handle both packaged components and fragments of documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature system must work with real XML programs and must be checked by all the groups that work on related XML standards.
